# From an area to composites

This page joins the steps of the previous pages into one script that takes an
area of interest (AOI) to composites on the MGRS grid squares that cover it.
s1bursts provides each step, and the script that joins them is yours to adapt.
The script below assumes that all squares lie in one UTM zone, as they do for
most areas. [The last section](#areas-across-a-utm-zone-boundary) adapts it
to an area across a zone boundary.

## Outline

Compositing is the only step that works one square at a time. Searching,
downloading and processing serve all squares at once, so they run once for
the whole area, and SNAP gets one batch of bursts that it can process in
parallel:

```{.python}
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))

# Once for the whole area
bursts = catalog.search(...)                     # every burst that reaches a square
catalog.download(bursts)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, ...)  # one batch, in the zone of the squares

# Once per square
for square in squares:
    square_rtc = ...                             # the products whose bursts reach it
    weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, ...)
```

The next three sections fill in these steps. Together, their code blocks form
the complete script. The
[Martigny tutorial](martigny-composite.qmd) runs the same script on real data.

## Find the bursts of every square

`MGRSGrid` lists the squares that the AOI touches. Its `resolution` is the
pixel size of the composites, so it is taken from the processing settings:

```{.python}
import shapely
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)

aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
config = RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20)
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=config.grid_spacing))

search_area = shapely.union_all([box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for square in squares])
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))
```

The search covers the squares, not the AOI. `MGRSGrid` includes every square
that the AOI touches, whole, and each composite covers its whole square. A
search of the AOI would miss a burst that reaches only the part of an edge
square outside the AOI, and that square would be composed from fewer
acquisitions without a warning. A later run would then skip the incomplete
composite as finished.

`search_area` joins the bounding boxes of the squares in longitude and
latitude, since the exact outline of a square has too many vertices for a
catalog query. A bounding box is slightly larger than its square, so no burst
is missed.

## Process in the zone of the squares

A composite accepts only products in the UTM zone of its square, so the bursts
are processed with that zone as `crs`, not with `crs="auto"`;
[Compositing](compositing.qmd#get-the-grid-squares) explains why. One batch
has one `crs`, so check first that all squares share a zone:

```{.python}
if len({square.crs for square in squares}) > 1:
    raise ValueError("The squares span several UTM zones; process each zone on its own.")
crs = squares[0].crs

catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=crs, config=config).raise_on_failure().products
```

To set how many bursts SNAP processes at once, see
[Run several jobs at once](processing.qmd#run-several-jobs-at-once).

## Compose each square

Each square is composed from the products whose bursts reach it.
`intersecting()` selects those bursts from the search result, and a product
belongs to a burst footprint by its `burst_id` and `sub_swath`:

```{.python}
from s1bursts.errors import CompositeError


def reaching(products, bursts, square):
    """Return the products whose burst footprint reaches the square."""
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    return [p for p in products if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]


failed = {}
for square in squares:
    square_rtc = reaching(rtc, bursts, square)
    if not square_rtc:
        continue  # no burst reaches the square
    try:
        weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
    except CompositeError as error:
        failed[square.mgrs_code] = error
```

Passing all products to every square would give the same composites, since a
product outside a square contributes nothing to it, but each product would be
read once per square.

Some squares cannot be composed, because of their own data. A square that no
burst reached in the time window has no products, so the loop skips it. A
burst footprint can also touch a square without a valid pixel in it, and if
that holds for all products of a square, the call raises an
`EmptyCompositeError`. Such an error concerns one square and is a
`CompositeError`, so the loop records it in `failed` and continues with the
next square. An error that every square would meet is not a `CompositeError`
and stops the loop: an `InconsistentInputsError` for products in another UTM
zone or at another pixel size, or a `ProductSettingsMismatchError` for
composites made with other settings.

A composite holds one polarization. For VV and VH, run the script once with
each.

Rerunning the script is cheap. Downloads, products and composites that exist
are skipped, so after a failure only the missing pieces are made.

## Add coherence

Coherence composites follow the same outline, with pairs in place of bursts,
and take the RTC products of the same dates as weights. A pair that starts at
the end of the window ends after it, so the search reaches beyond the window
by the baseline, and the bursts and pairs that start within the window are
kept, as in [Pair acquisitions](finding-and-downloading.qmd#pair-acquisitions).
These lines take the place of the search and of the download and processing
calls:

```{.python}
from datetime import timedelta

from s1bursts import CoherenceConfig

found = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
    time_range=TimeRange(window.start, window.end + timedelta(days=12)),
    intersects=search_area, polarization="VV",
))
bursts = found.within(window)
pairs = found.find_pairs(baseline=12).starting_within(window)
catalog.download([*bursts, *pairs]).raise_on_failure()

rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=crs, config=config).raise_on_failure().products
coh = processor.create_coherences(
    pairs, crs=crs, config=CoherenceConfig(grid_spacing=config.grid_spacing),
).raise_on_failure().products
```

`download()` fetches both acquisitions of each pair and every burst only once.
Each square's coherence is then composed with that square's RTC products:

```{.python}
for square in squares:
    square_coh = reaching(coh, bursts, square)
    if not square_coh:
        continue  # no pair reaches the square
    try:
        weighter.compose_coherence_lrw(
            square_coh, reaching(rtc, bursts, square), square, write_qa=True, time_range=window,
        )
    except CompositeError as error:
        failed[square.mgrs_code] = error
```

## Areas across a UTM zone boundary

Each UTM zone is gridded on its own, so for an AOI that crosses a zone
boundary, `MGRSGrid` returns squares of both zones, and they overlap along the
boundary. `box(5.9, 46.0, 6.1, 46.1)`, for example, crosses 6° E and gives four
squares in zone 31 and four in zone 32, among them 32TKR69, which covers half
of 31TGL29. Composing all of them gives that ground one composite in each zone.

The squares of each zone need their own processing batch, in their zone. Group
the squares by zone, and run the script for each group, with `zone_squares` in
place of `squares` and without the zone check:

```{.python}
from collections import defaultdict

squares_by_zone = defaultdict(list)
for square in squares:
    squares_by_zone[square.crs].append(square)

for crs, zone_squares in squares_by_zone.items():
    ...  # search, download, process and compose zone_squares as above
```

A burst near the boundary is found by the searches of both zones. It is
downloaded once and processed once per zone.

Another way, for any number of zones, is to run the whole script for each
square on its own: search the bounding box of the square, keep the bursts
`intersecting()` it, then download them, process them with `crs=square.crs`
and compose. Each search stays small, which suits an area whose zones hold
more bursts than one search returns. Neighboring squares share most of their
bursts, but each burst is still downloaded and processed only once per zone,
since the later squares find its files and skip them. The cost is
parallelism: each batch hands SNAP only the few bursts that are not processed
yet.
